sky.name: Sky
sky.description: The first four cells gather major celestial figures: Tinia, the supreme god comparable with Zeus and Jupiter; Cilens, often associated with Tinia; Thufltha, whose function remains debated; Nethuns, securely compared with Neptune and Poseidon; and Uni, a major goddess comparable with Juno and Hera.

water.name: Water
water.description: The next four cells include Tecum, an obscure figure connected with dedications around Lake Trasimeno; Lusal, whose reading and identity are debated; Nethuns, securely compared with Neptune and Poseidon; and Catha, an astral deity whose solar or lunar character is debated.

earth.name: Earth
earth.description: A terrestrial grouping connected with vegetation, boundaries, and earth-related divine powers. Its agricultural and boundary meanings are interpretive rather than fixed translations.

underworld.name: Underworld
underworld.description: A chthonic grouping of earth, protective, and underworld-associated names. It may relate to death, protection, and liminal passages, but individual meanings vary in certainty.

pars_familiaris.name: Pars Familiaris
pars_familiaris.description: The familiar or favorable side of the model, including names often read as domestic, attendant, or beneficent. Its omen value is part of the interpretive framework.

gall_bladder.name: Gall Bladder
gall_bladder.description: The bile reservoir is a charged divinatory area containing Tvnth, Maris, Laran, Letham, and Nethuns. Several identifications in this zone remain debated.

central_section.name: Central Section
central_section.description: The central zone contains Hercle, Maris, Letham, Metlvmth, and Tluscva. It combines better-documented divine names with obscure forms whose status remains uncertain.

pars_hostilis.name: Pars Hostilis
pars_hostilis.description: The hostile or unfavorable side of the model, including boundary, chthonic, and difficult-to-identify names. Its unfavorable force is an interpretive category.

back.name: Back
back.description: The back contains the Sun and Moon labels, commonly read as celestial anchors for the model's cosmological structure.

secure.label: Secure identification
secure.tooltip: The Etruscan deity is securely identified in current scholarship.

probable.label: Probable identification
probable.tooltip: The Etruscan deity identification is plausible but not final.

debated.label: Debated identification
debated.tooltip: Scholars disagree about the identification of this name.

unresolved.label: Unresolved
unresolved.tooltip: No secure identification is currently given for this form.

clear.label: Clear reading
clear.tooltip: The Etruscan glyphs are clearly inscribed and read.

debated.label: Debated reading
debated.tooltip: The form is visible, but its reading or word division is debated.

secure.label: Secure
secure.tooltip: The Greek or Roman match is well established in current scholarship.

proposed.label: Proposed
proposed.tooltip: The Greek or Roman match is one proposal among several; not consensus.

superseded.label: Superseded
superseded.tooltip: Older equivalence preserved here as scholarship history; not endorsed by recent work.

tinia.description: Supreme sky god and father of the Etruscan pantheon. Holds five cells on the liver — including the locative form tinsθ ‘in (the house) of Tinia’ at cell 22, where Nethuns appears as guest of Tinia. Central to the doctrine of the three lightning bolts (manubiae) and the sixteen-part heaven.

cilens.description: Deity in three cells (1, 16, 36); paired with Tinia in cell 1 and possibly with the locative Cilensl, ‘in (the house) of Cilens’, in cell 16. Pallottino 1956 first proposed equation with Marziano Capella's Nocturnus; Colonna 2012 reads Cilens as a catactonic (sub-earthly) divinity.

thufltha.description: Female deity present at cells 2, 20, 21. A Vulci dedication on a Bacco statuette (Buranelli 1989) pairs her with infero Suri, complicating older Fortuna / Tyche equations. The tinsθ θvf locative at cell 20 places Thufltha ‘in the house of Tinia’.

nethuns.description: Water and sea god in four cells (3, 7, 22, 28). Colonna 1991 distinguishes a ‘celestial’ Nethuns at cells 3 and 22, hosted in Tinia's house and possibly governing rain and atmospheric moisture, from the chthonic / aqueous Nethuns of cells 7 and 28 (consecrated, per Pliny, to the vesica fellea).

uni.description: Major state goddess of cities, birth, and sovereignty; some evidence also points to warlike and astral aspects, including comparisons with Astarte at Pyrgi.

mae.description: Obscure paired name in the Uni / Mae inscription at cell 4. Maras 2017 lists Mae among the deities attested only on the Liver of Piacenza; function and identification remain unresolved, and older equations with Roman Maius are not supported in recent scholarship.

tecvm.description: Obscure deity known almost exclusively from the liver and from dedications in the area around Lake Trasimeno. Colonna 1976-77 connected the cult with Cel and the Trasimeno sanctuaries; function on the liver remains debated.

lusal.description: Genitive form lvsl / lvsal at cells 6 and 34. Two readings: a deity Lusa (Maggiani 1982) or, per Colonna 1991, lv(r)s(l) — ‘of Lurs’, the prophetic god Lur. The Liber Linteus attestations are studied by van der Meer 2009; de Grummond 2014 reconstructs the cult from mirrors, dedications, and the linen book.
lusal.editorialNote: The reading itself is debated. Cell 6 (lvsal) is taken as fairly secure; cell 34 (lvsl velχ) is contested — vel(...) may also point to an eponymous god of Vulci (Torelli 1986).

catha.description: Astral deity, probably female (cells 8, 23). Maras 2017 still reads Catha as ‘a later counterpart of Cavatha, with marked solar features’, and Colonna 1991 links the Cathe Sans of the Orbetello mirror to a male solar Catha; against this, de Grummond 2008 argued for a lunar Catha at Pyrgi and Moore 2018 explicitly revisits the question. Solar, lunar, underworld, and childbirth associations all remain on the table.
catha.editorialNote: The older single-solar consensus has been complicated by lunar and chthonic readings, but Maras 2017 and Colonna 1991 still defend the solar interpretation.

fufluns.description: God of wine, inebriation, and vegetation cycles.

selvans.description: God of forests, pastures, and liminal lands or boundaries; venerated as tutor finium. Per Colonna 1991, the cell-17 inscription read pul by Maggiani may instead be tul, an abbreviation of the epithet tul(aras) — supporting Selvans's role as guardian of boundaries.

tluscva.description: Obscure form at cells 12, 33, 40. Maggiani 2011 treats Tluschva as chthonic divinity / divine collective, probably female; Maras 2017 reads them as ‘a group of goddesses, perhaps corresponding to Nymphs or Charites’ attested also at Caere (Sant'Antonio); Colonna 1991 alternatively proposed Tluscu as an epithet of Maris (the only true hapax of the liver). Stopponi 2012 connects the cult with the Fanum Voltumnae at Orvieto.

cels.description: Cel / Cels, earth goddess connected with chthonic forces. Colonna 1976-77 is the canonical study, linking Cel with the Trasimeno sanctuaries; the liver itself has been read as a model of Cel's body.

culsans.description: Double-faced god of doors and thresholds. Colonna 1991 analyses the northern orthography Culsans as a compound culś sans, ‘Cul the genitor’; the abbreviation cvl at cell 14 may stand for either Cul (Bagnoregio altar) or Culsans.

alpans.description: Alpan / Alpans paired with Cul / Culsans at cell 14. Colonna 1991 argues that alpan is originally an appellative meaning ‘the good / well-disposed’, semantically equivalent to Latin manus — used for chthonic divinities in eufemistic register. So alp here functions as an epithet of Cul, comparable to Janus being called bonus and manus.

vetis.description: Catactonic deity at cell 15. Maras 2017 reads Vetis as the Etruscan substitution for Apollo on the Liver, derived from Latin Vedius (a variant of Veiovis); Colonna 2012 places Vetis with Cilens among the catactonic divinities of the hostile sector.

pul.description: Cell 17. Maggiani 1982 reads pul, interpreted as ‘sky’ in opposition to metlum at cell 38. Colonna 1991 questions the reading, arguing that the first letter could be t rather than p, and proposes tul(aras) as an epithet of Selvans (tutor finium).
pul.editorialNote: The reading itself is contested between Maggiani's pul and Colonna's tul.

lasl.description: Lasa / Lasl at cell 19. Female divine attendant often linked with Turan; fate and service roles are attested in mirror iconography. The Roman Lares are not a satisfactory match.

maris.description: Important but obscure deity at cells 26, 30, 39 (cells 30+39 communicate around the processus papillaris). Often represented as a child or youth in Etruscan evidence; Maras 2017 records Mariś at Clusium as ‘a divine child bearing the name of the Latin-Italic Mars’. At cell 26 the reading marisl laθ — once read as an unknown epithet — was revised by Maggiani in discussion to marisl lar, supporting an analogy with the Roman Lar familiaris (Colonna 1991).
maris.editorialNote: Maris shares an etymology with Latin-Italic Mars but is functionally distinct from the Roman war-god; the older identification of Maris with Mars in cult and role is no longer accepted (Simon 2006; Krauskopf 2013; Maras 2017).

tvnth.description: Uncertain deity at cell 25, in the gall bladder zone. Maras 2017 lists Tvnth among the deities attested only on the Liver; no firm identification has emerged in recent scholarship.

hercle.description: Major Etruscan god, equivalent of Herakles and Hercules, with protective and oracular associations. In Etruria treated as a god from the beginning, not as a hero.

metlvmth.description: Cell 38. Colonna 1991 reads metlumθ as a locative meaning ‘in the city / urbs’ — qualifying the adjacent Lethams of cell 37 as the ‘Lethams in the city’, parallel to the divine genitive sintagms of the Liber Linteus.
metlvmth.editorialNote: Per Colonna 1991, cells 37 and 38 form a single inscription leθam(sl) metlumθ — not two independent deity names.

letham.description: Lethams (correct form per the Capua tile gen. ledamsul; Colonna 1991 corrects the earlier Letham). Five cells (11, 18, 27, 32, 37) make this the most ‘ubiquitous’ deity of the liver — possibly genius-like, occupying both right and left lobes. Gender and sphere remain debated.
letham.editorialNote: Maggiani 1982 wrote ‘Letham’; Colonna 1991 demonstrated that the correct form is ‘Lethams’, on the evidence of the Capua tile.

velch.description: vel(...) at cell 34, paired with Lvsl. Colonna 1991 cites Torelli 1986 in suggesting Vel(...) may name an eponymous god of Vulci rather than a fire / metalworking deity comparable to Vulcan. The fire-god reading remains tentative.

satres.description: Obscure deity at cell 35. Function and identification remain debated; the form satres / satre is also attested in the Liber Linteus from Zagreb.
satres.editorialNote: The older equivalence with Saturn is preserved here as scholarship history; it is no longer treated as secure (Maggiani 1982, Krauskopf 2013).

usil.description: The Etruscan sun-god, securely identified. On the back of the liver (cell 42) usils marks the solar pole of the cosmological structure.

tiur.description: Tiur / Tivr, moon deity or moon / month term. Cell 41 marks the lunar pole of the back, opposite Usil. Sannibale 2018 published a bronze crescent (CII 2610 bis) with a fresh dedication to Tiur, confirming the divine status of the term.
